children: New data from Eli Lilly show the world's largest pharmaceutical company continues to bet heavily on its weight-loss drug pipeline, offering a clearer picture of how its next-generation treatments could reduce the broader burden of obesity.

A recent analysis of a late-stage trial suggests that Eli Lilly's oral GLP-1 drug, Foundayo, lowers the long-term risk of Type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. The 72-week trial evaluated three doses of Foundayo against a placebo in adults living with obesity or weight-related health conditions.

Using 10-year predictive modeling based on the trial data, researchers found that the highest dose reduced the predicted risk of developing Type 2 diabetes by up to 57% and cardiovascular disease by 18% compared with a placebo. The results imply Foundayo could reduce long-term healthcare spending by treating obesity while preventing secondary complications like Type 2 diabetes and heart disease, according to Lilly.

The findings cap off a double dose of major news for Lilly. Late Wednesday, the company also reported clinical trial results for EloraTZP, an experimental drug combining tirzepatide-the active ingredient in Zepbound and Mounjaro-with pipeline candidate eloralintide.
Unlike tirzepatide, which targets the GIP and GLP-1 receptors to control blood sugar and appetite, eloralintide mimics the hormone amylin, which the pancreas releases alongside insulin.

A head-to-head trial showed EloraTZP helped patients with Type 2 diabetes lose an average of 23.3% of their body weight, compared with just 14.8% weight loss in patients taking Lilly's tirzepatide, the company said. That translated to 54.1 pounds and 34.4 pounds, respectively, over the course of 48 weeks.

Citi analyst Graham Parry highlighted that while weight-loss efficacy was competitive with Novo Nordisk's own amylin drug combo, CagriSema, and Lilly's own retatrutide, the trial saw a higher dropout rate due to side effects than currently available treatments.

However, most discontinuations occurred while scaling up the dose, leading Parry to suggest Lilly can mitigate the problem in a late-stage trial expected to launch by year-end, which will feature a more gradual dosing schedule.

Widely viewed as the leader in the weight-loss drug market, Lilly is aiming to deepen its advantage. The pharmaceutical giant has been exploring novel formulations and alternative delivery methods, most notably daily oral medications, to solidify its foothold.

While Lilly's oral Foundayo gained approval in April for weight management, it still lags behind Novo's oral Wegovy in prescription volume. Novo benefits from a first-mover advantage, though Lilly previously demonstrated it could overcome a similar head start in the injectable market.
In its 23rd week on the market, Foundayo logged 47,000 prescriptions-a figure Jefferies analyst Akash Tewari noted is well behind oral Wegovy's 162,000 prescriptions at the same point in its launch.
That isn't cause for alarm just yet-Tewari noted that Lilly remains confident it simply takes time to build awareness for a new drug or brand.

Offsetting that slow start, however, is strong demand for Lilly's Zepbound KwikPen. Growth has been driven by a nationwide initiative launched in July, which allows eligible Medicare Part D patients to get covered GLP-1 weight-loss drugs for a flat $50 monthly copay.
